assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength lattice idea and developed by Ye into systems at the 10^-18 level, redefined what a clock can do. They give a stringent test of relativistic time dilation at centimetre scales, search sensitivity for variation of constants and dark matter, and are the leading candidates for a redefinition of the second. This is atomic physics where precision, control and theory (atomic structure, polarisabilities, blackbody shifts) meet cleanly.
assessment.attribution: The magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice-clock demonstration are clearly Katori's; Ye's JILA group drove the clock to its present stability and to many-body (spin-polarised Fermi gas) operation. A two-person prize looks fair. Contributions of comb and ultrastable-laser work (Hall, Hansch, already honoured in 2005) are credited elsewhere.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) confirm the performance, and the interpretation is stable. Timing is good: the technology is mature and the redefinition of the second is still pending, which does not weaken the physics case.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would rather prefer to recognise ion clocks (Al+ and others) alongside lattice clocks.
Declared interest: I work in atomic theory and know parts of this field personally, though without a direct collaboration with the credited names that I am aware of.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, followed by its realisation in HgTe quantum wells, opened a whole class of topological phases protected by symmetry. The conceptual originality is high and the impact extends to spintronics, topological superconductors and materials discovery.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the theoretical framework, with Z2 classification; Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposed HgTe and Molenkamp's group delivered the decisive experiment in 2007. Credit is not entirely clean because of the closely related 3D topological insulator work (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore, Balents; Zhang, Hasan) and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are not in the credited names for this entry.
assessment.maturity: Strong independent confirmation in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and 3D materials by ARPES; the field is more than 15 years old and stable. Recognition is timely, even somewhat overdue relative to the 2016 prize which covered topological phase transitions.
uncertainties: Allocation between the 2D quantum spin Hall and the 3D topological insulator discoveries is unresolved.
The omission of the proposers of HgTe as the platform among the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms turned the laser-cooling revolution into precision metrology: measurements of gravity, gravity gradients, the fine-structure constant and tests of the equivalence principle, with new prospects for gravitational-wave and dark-matter detection. It is a clean example of a quantum-mechanical principle becoming a measuring instrument.
assessment.attribution: Bordé's theoretical work on atom interferometers with light pulses, Pritchard's first atom interferometers (with diffraction gratings and light), and Kasevich and Chu's light-pulse gravimeter are all decisive. Chu already held a prize for laser cooling, and a three-way allocation among these names seems defensible; Chu's or Chapman's role is not in the supplied credit list, so I treat it as an unresolved attribution point.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many groups and used in commercial and field gravimeters; precision tests are ongoing. Further large-scale experiments (long baseline) are still under way, but the core achievement is mature.
uncertainties: Allocation of credit among the pioneering experimental groups (Pritchard, Mlynek, Kasevich-Chu, Bordé) is contested.
Some of the strongest applications (gravitational-wave detection, fundamental-physics tests) are still prospective.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum logic with trapped ions and the subsequent experimental implementations of gates, entanglement and algorithms are one of the foundations of quantum information science, and they rest on a deep understanding of atomic structure and light-matter interaction.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller supplied the theoretical blueprint in 1995 and Blatt's group performed leading realisations of the gate set and multi-ion entanglement. Wineland's earlier recognition in 2012 (for ion manipulation) overlaps with this topic, and the other experimental pioneers (Monroe, Wineland group at NIST) are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many groups and now commercial platforms. The discovery is mature, though part of the field has been recognised in 2012 and 2022, which weighs against its marginal novelty.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize for trapped-ion control and the 2022 quantum-information prize.
Whether Monroe's contributions would need to be allocated, which the credited names do not allow.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of flat bands at the magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity opened the field of moire materials and twistronics, with a rapidly growing set of tunable strongly correlated platforms.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald's continuum model predicted the magic angle, and Jarillo-Herrero's group delivered the decisive experiment; the three-name configuration is natural, though other theorists (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto; Suarez Morell) and experimentalists (Dean, Yacoby, Efetov and others) are involved.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by several groups and rich follow-up, but the nature of the superconducting pairing remains debated, and sample-to-sample variability persists. Timing is on the early side for the full understanding, though the discovery itself is solid.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still unsettled.
Credit among the early theory papers on twisted-bilayer flat bands is not entirely settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation of Hubbard-type models with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, including the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and later single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopes, offers controllable many-body systems with a direct link to atomic physics and condensed-matter theory.
assessment.attribution: Zoller with Jaksch and others proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation; Greiner and Bloch carried out the Mott transition experiment (Greiner with Hansch and Bloch) and developed the quantum gas microscope. The proposal by Jaksch and the roles of Hansch and Esslinger are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Extremely well confirmed and the field is mature, with active growth. Some of the targeted physical problems (high-temperature superconductivity in the Fermi-Hubbard model) remain out of reach, so the full scientific payoff is not yet realised.
uncertainties: Incomplete credit list (Jaksch, Hansch, Esslinger, Kasevich among others).
Overlap with the 2001 and 2012 recognition of atomic gases and control of quantum systems.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The concept of a photonic band gap, proposed independently by Yablonovitch and John in 1987, brought band-structure thinking to light and led to photonic crystals, photonic-crystal fibres and nanocavities, with a large influence on nanophotonics and quantum optics.
assessment.attribution: Yablonovitch (inhibited spontaneous emission) and John (localisation of light) are the conceptual originators, and Joannopoulos built the theory and the design framework for the structures; Russell (photonic crystal fibre) and Noda (nanocavities) are also in the supplied list. A prize could be framed around the concept alone, which is easiest with these three.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed (first microwave and then optical band gaps), with commercial fibres and nanocavity devices. The discovery is mature enough, if slightly late, and its direct impact on fundamental physics, as distinct from technology, is less clear.
uncertainties: Weighting of fundamental discovery versus technology.
Omitting Russell and Noda from the three-person configuration.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The proposal to use squeezed vacuum to beat the standard quantum limit in interferometry and its experimental realisation have become part of the gravitational-wave detectors' operation, a case where quantum optics changed a major instrument.
assessment.attribution: Caves provided the theoretical proposal in 1981, Kimble's group made the first squeezed states of light by four-wave mixing and later techniques (with Slusher at Bell Labs), and Schnabel brought the technology to long-baseline detectors. Slusher and the Bell Labs group are not in the credited names, so the claim of a clean configuration is not firm.
assessment.maturity: Squeezed light is now routine in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600, so confirmation and use are strong; the physics is mature, but the 2017 prize for gravitational waves already honoured the detector context.
uncertainties: Credit for the first experimental squeezed light is not fully captured by the credited names.
Part of the significance flows through the 2017 gravitational-wave prize.
